It was the unmistakable sound of a hidden mechanism, a clear sign that the pirates had prepared their lair for just such a pursuit.
“That sound!” Arthur exclaimed, his face grim in the green glow of the instrument panel. “They have sealed the entrance!”
“Be ther saints, they’ve trapped themselves like rats in a cage!” cried Gus from the pilot’s seat. “But they’ve locked us out, too!”
“What do we do now, Arthur?” asked Sam, his steady gaze fixed on the black opening before them. “We cannot simply wait for them to come out.”
“No,” replied the young inventor, his mind already racing through possibilities. “We will not wait. If Captain Jones will not come out to us, then we must go in to him!”
“But the gate, Masther Arthur! It sounded like solid iron.”
“It is likely just that, Gus. We cannot ram it, for that might damage the Triton’s prow and spring a leak in this pressure. But we do not need to ram it.”
A confident smile played upon Arthur’s lips. He went to a large locker built into the bulkhead and swung it open. Inside were various tools and strange looking implements of his own design.
“We will cut our way in,” he declared, pulling out a long, heavy device with two tanks attached by armored hoses. “This is our key. The powerful oxy-hydrogen torch!”
“Holy smoke!” exclaimed Sam. “Will that cut through solid iron under water?”
“It will cut through a battleship’s armor plate under water!” Arthur said with pride. “Sam, you will come with me. We will need our electric diving suits. Gus, you will remain at the helm. Keep the Triton steady and the searchlight fixed upon the gate. We must see what we are doing.”
“Aye, aye, Masther Arthur!” replied the Irishman, his hands tightening on the controls. “I’ll hold her as steady as a rock.”
The Triton crept forward into the black maw of the cave. The water, so clear outside, was now inky and opaque beyond the cone of their light. The sounds of the submersible’s electric motors echoed strangely off unseen walls. In a few moments, the searchlight beam found its target.
It was a massive iron grille, bolted directly into the stone of the cave. The bars were as thick as a man’s arm, and it stretched from wall to wall, disappearing into the dark water below and the arched ceiling above.
“There it is,” Arthur said. “There is no way around it. Prepare the diving suits.”
In a few minutes, Arthur and Sam were clad in their remarkable diving costumes. These were not the clumsy, canvas and brass contraptions of the navy, but sleek, jointed suits of aluminum alloy, powered by small, silent electric motors in the packs on their backs. Small propellers at their feet would allow them to maneuver with the grace of fish, and their helmets were equipped with powerful electric lamps and telephonic communicators.
The lower airlock hissed open. Water swirled into the small chamber. Arthur and Sam, carrying the heavy torch between them, stepped out into the cold, black water of the cave.
“Gus, can you hear us?” spoke Arthur into his mouthpiece.
“Clear as a bell, sor!” came the reply through their earpieces.
“Keep the light steady. We are approaching the gate now.”
Propelling themselves forward, they soon reached the iron barrier. It was even more formidable up close. Rust and sea-growth covered it, but the core was solid, unforgiving iron.
“Here we go, Sam,” said Arthur. “Hold your position.”
Arthur aimed the nozzle of the torch at one of the thick vertical bars. He pressed a stud on the handle. With a loud hiss that was clearly audible even through the water and their helmets, a brilliant, piercing blue-white flame erupted from the nozzle. The water around it instantly boiled and vaporized in a churning cloud of steam.
The effect upon the iron was immediate. The spot where the flame touched glowed cherry red, then white-hot. Molten metal began to drip away like wax, falling into the darkness below.
From the darkness beyond the gate, a gruff voice shouted, muffled by the stone and water. “What’s that noise?”
“They hear us!” Sam said into his communicator.
“Keep working, Masther Arthur!” Gus urged from the Triton. “They know we’re here now!”
Arthur moved the torch slowly, steadily, cutting a line through the thick bar. The intense light illuminated the cavern on the other side in flickering, hellish flashes. They could make out startled figures, pirates with pistols and cutlasses in hand, staring in disbelief at the impossible flame that was eating through their defenses.
A second voice yelled. “They are cutting through the gate! Stop them!”
A long pike was suddenly thrust through the bars, aimed at Arthur. Sam, ever vigilant, batted it aside with a gauntleted hand. The pirates cursed, but they could not reach the two men in their strange diving armor.
Arthur finished the first cut. He moved to the other side of the same bar and began to cut again. The work was slow, but progress was certain. The pirates on the other side grew more frantic. A pistol was fired, but the bullet merely glanced off the stone wall with a harmless whine. They were safe for the moment.
“One more ought to do it!” Arthur grunted, sweat beading on his brow inside the helmet. He started a cut on a second, adjacent bar. The hissing of the torch and the boiling of the water filled the cave with a deafening roar.
Finally, with a tremendous, groaning screech of tortured metal, the section of the gate they had been working on gave way. The two severed bars and the cross-braces connecting them sagged, bent, and then plunged into the unseen depths of the cave floor with a mighty splash and a clang that echoed for a long time.
“We are through!” cried Sam in triumph.
“Back to the Triton! Quickly!” Arthur commanded.
They propelled themselves back to the waiting submersible and climbed inside the airlock. As the water was pumped out, they could hear the pirates shouting in alarm and confusion.
“Begorra, ye did it!” Gus yelled as they emerged into the control room, pulling off their helmets. “I saw the whole thing! It was a grand sight!”
“There is no time to waste,” said Arthur, taking his place at the forward viewport. “Gus, take us in. Slowly and carefully.”
The Triton glided through the newly made gap in the iron gate. The searchlight cut a swath through the gloom, revealing a cavern of immense size. The ceiling, lost in darkness far above, dripped with massive stalactites. The cave opened up into a wide, natural harbor, with a stone ledge on one side that served as a crude dock.
And there, stacked high upon the ledge, were the stolen munitions. Crate after crate of rifles, ammunition, and cannon shells, all bearing the marks of the United States Navy.
“There’s the treasure,” Sam said grimly. “But where are the pirates?”
“Hiding,” Arthur replied, scanning the shadows. “They have the advantage of terrain. We must be cautious. Bring the Triton alongside that ledge.”
Gus maneuvered the submersible expertly, bringing its flank gently against the stone dock. The main hatch was opened, and a ramp extended. The air was cool and damp, filled with the smell of brine and wet stone.
“I will go first,” Arthur said, picking up his electric rifle, a sleek weapon of his own invention that fired concentrated bolts of electrical force. “Sam, Gus, cover me.”
“Be careful, Masther Arthur,” said Gus, brandishing a similar, though smaller, electric pistol.
Arthur stepped onto the ledge. The cavern was as quiet as a tomb. The only sound was the gentle lapping of water against the Triton’s hull and the distant drip, drip, drip of water from the ceiling. He took a few steps forward, his rifle at the ready.
Suddenly, a shot rang out!
A bullet ricocheted off a stalagmite near Arthur’s head, showering him with stone chips.
“Ambush!” yelled Sam, as he and Gus leaped out onto the dock, taking cover behind a stack of crates.
From behind pillars of rock and the tall stacks of munitions, a dozen pirates appeared, firing their pistols and muskets. The cavern erupted with the roar of gunpowder and the flash of muzzles. Bullets whizzed through the air and spanged off the Triton’s hull.
“The rascals!” cried Gus, firing his electric pistol. A bolt of blue energy shot out and struck a pirate in the shoulder. The man howled and dropped his weapon, his arm going numb and useless.
Arthur took aim and fired his own rifle. His shot was true, striking a charging buccaneer in the chest. The man was not killed, but he was thrown backwards as if by a giant’s fist, his entire body convulsing from the powerful shock. He lay on the ground, twitching and unable to rise.
The pirates, who had never faced such weapons, fell back in confusion and fear. Their lead balls were having little effect on the men of the Triton, who were well-protected by the crates and the submersible itself.
“Press the attack!” Arthur shouted. “Don’t give them time to reload!”
The three heroes advanced, firing their electric weapons. The pirates were no match for this futuristic assault. Several more were disabled by the crackling energy bolts, falling to the stone floor or retreating deeper into the shadows of the immense cavern. The tide of the battle was turning decisively in their favor.
Just then, a figure emerged from behind the largest stack of munitions. It was Captain Jones himself, his face a mask of fury and desperation. He was not holding a pistol, but a flaming torch.
“Look!” cried Arthur, his blood running cold. “The munitions!”
Captain Jones, seeing that his men were defeated and his capture was imminent, had resorted to the ultimate act of spite. He ran toward a pile of crates clearly marked with warnings of high explosives.
“He means to blow us all to kingdom come!” gasped Sam.
“Stop, you madman!” Arthur yelled, breaking from cover and sprinting across the slick cavern floor.
Jones reached the crates of blasting powder and naval mines. He turned, a crazed grin on his face, and held the torch high.
“Stay back!” he screamed, his voice echoing unnaturally in the vast space. “One step closer, and I’ll send us all to Davy Jones’s locker! If I can’t have me prize, no one will!”
Arthur skidded to a halt, a mere thirty feet from the pirate captain. Sam and Gus held their fire, knowing that a stray shot could detonate the entire stockpile and bring the roof of the cave down upon them all. The air was thick with tension. The sputtering torch cast a flickering, dancing light on the pirate’s wild eyes.
Arthur knew he could not risk shooting his rifle. The electrical discharge might be enough to set off the powder. He had to think of another way. His eyes darted around the cavern, and then to his belt, where several of his smaller inventions were clipped.
His hand fell upon a small, pistol-like device, no bigger than his palm. It was his voltaic paralyzer, a short-range weapon designed for stunning, not destruction. It was his only chance.
“It’s over, Jones!” Arthur said, his voice calm and steady, trying to distract the pirate. “Surrender, and you will be treated fairly.”
“Never!” shrieked Jones, and he began to lower the torch toward an open keg of black powder.
Arthur raised the small device. He had no time to aim carefully. He fired.
A crackling arc of blue energy, thinner and more focused than the rifle’s blast, leaped forth. It struck the pirate captain squarely in the chest.
Jones’s body went instantly rigid. A strangled cry escaped his lips. His muscles locked, and his eyes bulged. The torch fell from his nerveless grasp, tumbling end over end through the air.
It landed on the stone floor, a mere foot from the open powder keg, and sputtered.
“The torch!” Sam yelled, and without a second’s hesitation, he rushed forward and stamped out the sputtering flame with his heavy boot, grinding the embers into harmless dust.
A collective sigh of relief went through the cavern. Captain Jones, his body still trembling from the paralyzing shock, collapsed to the ground, conscious but unable to move a muscle. Seeing their captain fall and their terrible plan thwarted, the rest of the pirates threw down their arms and surrendered, their faces a mixture of terror and awe.
“We have him!” exclaimed Arthur, rushing forward to ensure the munitions were truly safe. “And the cargo is secure.”
“Begorra, we’ve put an end to his villainy for good this time!” Gus declared, kicking a pistol away from a surrendering pirate. “He’ll not be plaguing the seas again for a long, long time.”
They worked quickly, tying up the stunned Captain Jones and his crew of scoundrels with rope found in the cave. The pirates offered no resistance, their spirit utterly broken.
An hour later, the prisoners were all secured in the Triton’s small but strong brig. Arthur stood on the stone ledge, surveying the vast hoard of stolen government property.
“We cannot move all of this ourselves,” he said to Sam. “We will have to notify the authorities. But first, we will deal with the Sea Serpent.”
“What are you going to do, Arthur?”
“We will disable her rudder and engine, and take her crew prisoner as well. Then we will tow the brig as a prize back to the nearest port and hand Captain Jones and his entire operation over to the navy. His career of piracy is over.”
With the prisoners secure and their mission accomplished, Arthur turned the Triton back toward the mouth of the cave. The submersible glided through the broken gate and out into the bright morning light.
The rising sun glinted off the waves. The Sea Serpent sat at anchor, her remaining crew unaware of the fate that had befallen their captain. Their perilous night was over, and a great victory had been won. Arthur set a course for the pirate brig, a determined look on his face, ready for the final act of this grand adventure.

“We have no proof of your identity. Your craft is unknown and your story is fantastic. You are in command of a vessel of war of unknown origin. Under the articles of naval law, I must treat you as a hostile actor. Cast off your tow and prepare to be boarded. This is your final warning.”

“They leave us no choice,” he said, his voice grim. “We cannot lose the Triton.”

“What are we to do?” Sam asked, his face tense.

“We must abandon the prize,” Arthur announced. “Our own safety, and the safety of this vessel, must come first. Gus, release the magnetic clamps! On my mark!”

“But the pirates! The Sea Serpent!” Gus protested. “We’re to let them have all the credit?”

“They can have the credit, and the pirates too!” Arthur retorted. “We will live to sail another day. It is a bitter pill, but we must swallow it. Prepare to release!”

“Now, Gus!” Arthur ordered.

Gus threw a heavy lever set near the stern. With a loud clang, the electromagnetic tow clamps disengaged. The heavy cables splashed into the sea, and the Sea Serpent, suddenly free, drifted to a stop.

“All hands below!” Arthur yelled. “Prepare for an emergency dive!”

Sam and Gus scrambled down the hatch, sealing it tightly behind them. Arthur was the last one in, securing the main hatch of the conning tower just as another, larger gun on the Dauntless flashed.

“Dive! Full power to the dive planes!”

The Triton shuddered as its ballast tanks flooded with incredible speed. The submersible tilted forward, its nose dipping beneath the waves. A geyser of water erupted nearby as the cruiser’s second shell struck the water precisely where they had been moments before. The shockwave buffeted them, but the Triton’s hull was strong.

“Captain Harrington was only doing his duty as he saw it,” Arthur said, though his voice was laced with frustration. “The situation was, I admit, highly irregular.”

“Irregular or not, we’ve lost our prize and are now wanted men,” Sam said grimly. “What is our next move, Arthur?”

Arthur Worthington stared into the glowing sonar screen, which showed only the empty expanse of the deep sea around them. The anger and frustration on his face slowly gave way to a look of intense concentration, the look of an inventor faced with a new and challenging problem.

“They called our story fantastic,” he said quietly, a flicker of a smile touching his lips. “They do not know the half of it. We cannot surface near any major port now. We will be hunted.”

He turned from the screen to face his two loyal companions.

“Our next move,” he declared, his eyes shining with a familiar adventurous light, “is to find a place where the Royal Navy will never think to look for us. And from there, we will find a way to clear our names and prove to the world what the Triton can do. Set a course for the south, Mr. Reynard. We have a long journey ahead of us.”

Sam nodded, his own spirits rising at his friend’s indomitable will. He turned to the helm, his hands moving surely over the controls. The Triton banked gently, turning its nose toward the vast, unexplored waters of the South Atlantic, leaving the baffled warship and its captured prize far behind on the surface, already a fading memory in the wake of a new and greater adventure.

“Aye, aye, Masther Frank!” Barney yelled, already shinnying up a palm tree with a thick coil of rope over his shoulder. “We’ll tie this bird down so a hurricane couldn’t move her!”

The roar of the wind and the crashing of waves on the outer reef was deafening.

Barney had been tasked with watching him, but the Irishman was called away to help Pomp with a line that had come loose from the airship’s stern.

“Stay put, ye divil!” Barney had roared at Murdock. “If ye so much as poke yer nose out, I’ll tie ye to a tree for the crabs to find!”

This was the chance Murdock had been waiting for. He was a creature of cunning and opportunity, and he saw his opening in the heart of the tempest. The roar of the storm covered the sound of his movements.

He knew that the small service hatch near the engine room, used for venting exhaust, was often left unlatched. If he could get inside, he could sabotage the dynamo, or worse, set a fire. In the confusion, he might even be able to steal the airship.

He reached the hull of the floating machine, his fingers scrabbling for a handhold on the wet, slippery metal. He found the hatch. As he had gambled, it was not dogged down. With a surge of desperate strength, he pulled it open and squeezed inside, disappearing into the dark belly of the beast.

It was Pomp who first noticed something was amiss. While struggling to re-secure the stern line, he caught a flicker of movement out of the corner of his eye. He saw the service hatch, which he knew should be closed, swinging free in the wind.

“Masther Frank!” he bellowed, his voice barely carrying over the storm. “Someone’s gotten aboard! The aft hatch is open!”

Frank’s head snapped around. His eyes went instantly to Murdock’s tent. It was empty.

“Murdock!” he cried. “He’s inside the Pegasus! He’ll wreck the engines! Barney, Pomp, with me! Tom, stay here and guard the camp!”

“I’ll do more than that!” the detective shouted back, pulling his service revolver from his coat. “I will make sure he does not come out this way!”

Frank, Barney and Pomp scrambled aboard the lurching deck of the airship. The deck was awash, and they had to hold onto the railing to keep from being swept overboard. They plunged into the interior of the vessel, the sudden quiet of the cabin a stark contrast to the maelstrom outside.

“He’ll have gone for the engine room,” Frank said, his voice grim. “He knows that’s the heart of the ship. We must stop him.”

They raced down the narrow corridors, their footsteps echoing on the metal floors. When they reached the engine room, they found the heavy steel door barred from the inside.

“He’s locked himself in!” Barney roared, throwing his considerable weight against the door. It did not budge. “The cowardly snake!”

From within came the sound of crashing metal, followed by a high-pitched, triumphant laugh.

“You’re too late, you fools!” Murdock’s voice screamed from the other side. “I’ve smashed the primary regulator! In a few minutes, the dynamo will overload and explode! You’ll all be blown to kingdom come!”

Frank’s face went pale. He knew Murdock was not bluffing. An overloaded dynamo would indeed rupture with the force of a bomb, tearing the Pegasus to pieces.

“There’s no time to break down the door!” he yelled. “Barney, Pomp, follow me! There’s another way in!”

He led them to a small storage closet that backed onto the engine room. On the wall was a maintenance panel, held in place by six heavy bolts.

“Behind this panel is the main power conduit,” Frank explained rapidly. “If we can get it open, there is just enough room for a man to squeeze through into the engine room. Barney, your tools!”

The big Irishman produced a heavy wrench from his belt. He and Pomp fell upon the bolts with a desperate fury. The metal screeched in protest as they worked. Outside, the storm raged. Inside, a madman was counting down the seconds to their destruction.

“Hurry!” Frank urged, listening to the rising whine of the machinery through the wall. “The dynamo is already starting to overload!”

With a final groan, the last bolt gave way. They pulled the heavy panel aside, revealing a dark, narrow space filled with thick, insulated cables.

“I’m the smallest,” Pomp said, already stripping off his coat. “I’ll go!”

“Be careful, Pomp,” Frank warned. “He will be armed.”

“Don’t you worry ‘bout me, Masther Frank,” the brave coon replied. With a determined look, he squeezed into the opening and vanished into the darkness.

For a moment, there was only the sound of the storm and the terrifying shriek of the overloaded dynamo. Then, from the engine room, came a startled shout from Murdock, a crash, and the sound of a struggle. A pistol shot rang out, deafeningly loud in the confined space.

“Pomp!” Barney bellowed, making to follow him.

“Wait!” Frank cried, holding him back.

Another moment of terrible silence. Then, the high-pitched whine of the dynamo began to decrease. A loud clank was heard, as of a lever being thrown. The immediate danger was over.

The lock on the engine room door clicked, and the door swung open. Pomp stood there, breathing heavily. His sleeve was torn and there was a powder burn on his arm, but he was grinning. Behind him, on the floor, lay Martin Murdock, unconscious, with a nasty lump swelling on his forehead. A heavy spanner lay beside him.

“He didn’t expect me comin’ from behind,” Pomp said simply. “I hit him before he knew what was what. Then I shut down the dynamo.”

“Faith, an’ ye’re a hero, Pomp!” Barney cried, clapping him on the back so hard he nearly fell over.

Frank rushed to the control panel. “You were just in time,” he said, examining the gauges. “Another minute and the whole thing would have gone up. You saved our lives, Pomp. All of our lives.”

They dragged the unconscious Murdock out of the engine room and bound him securely with rope. This time, there would be no tent. They confined him to the same storeroom he had occupied before, but this time, they chained him to a steel support beam. His escape attempts were at an end.

When the storm finally broke the next morning, it left behind a world washed clean. The sun rose into a clear blue sky. The crew of the Pegasus, exhausted but triumphant, surveyed the damage. A few of the mooring lines had snapped, and the camp on the beach was a wreck, but the airship herself, thanks to their efforts and Pomp’s bravery, was largely unharmed.

Frank gathered his friends in the main cabin. His face was set and resolute.

“This settles it,” he said, his voice quiet but firm. “Murdock is too dangerous, and his knowledge is too great a threat to leave to chance. We can no longer think of this as a simple chase. It has become a duty. We are going to the Hawaiian Islands. We will find that outpost, and we will find the truth.”

A cheer went up from Barney and Pomp. Tom Reynard nodded in solemn agreement.

“What will we do if the key fits, Masther Frank?” Barney asked. “What if the whole mad story is true?”

Frank looked out the viewport at the endless horizon. A strange light, a mixture of scientific curiosity and the pure spirit of adventure, shone in his eyes.

“Then,” the young inventor replied, “we will take this flying machine to the end of the world. We will sail her into the heart of Erebus itself, and we will bring Professor Moriarty and his entire city of villains to justice.”

Two hours later, the engines of the Pegasus hummed to life. The great helices spun, churning the air into a blur. Rising majestically from the tranquil lagoon, the airship soared into the sky, leaving the tiny atoll of Aethelred’s Folly dwindling behind them. She turned her nose to the northeast, toward the distant Hawaiian chain, a silver arrow aimed at the heart of a new and monstrous mystery. The perils of the chase were behind them, but the perils of discovery, more profound and terrible than any they had yet imagined, lay waiting in the unknown skies ahead.

Below, the ocean rolled on in an unbroken sheet of sapphire, its rhythm a constant, soothing murmur that did little to calm the excited tension within the cabin of the Pegasus.

Inside, Frank Reade, Jr., stood before a large chart of the Pacific islands spread across the main table. His brow was furrowed in concentration, his keen eyes tracing the lines of longitude and latitude. Tom Reynard, the detective, stood beside him, a pipe held thoughtfully in his hand.

“According to my calculations, we should make landfall on the island of Hawaii in another two days,” Frank announced, tapping a point on the chart. “The question is, what do we do when we get there? It is a large island, full of mountains and jungles.”

“The papers we took from Murdock were sparse on details,” Reynard said, puffing a cloud of smoke. “He was clearly a subordinate, given just enough information to do his job, and no more. The only real clues are the name ‘Erebus’ and that peculiar key.”

“Faith, an’ it’s a queer-lookin’ key at that,” chimed in Barney, who was polishing his favorite rifle nearby. “Looks more like a gear from some divil’s own clock than a key for a door.”

Pomp, who had been quietly ensuring all the ship’s chronometers were in perfect sync, looked up. “A clockwork lock, perhaps,” he suggested. “A mechanism that requires a specific pattern of turns to open. It would be very difficult to pick.”

“An excellent thought, Pomp!” Frank exclaimed. “That fits with the cunning of a man like Moriarty. Everything he does is a puzzle, a machine. His entire criminal empire is said to run with the precision of a watch.”

Frank picked up the key. It was heavy, made of a strange, non-tarnishing alloy, with teeth cut at irregular intervals. It did not look like it was meant for a simple tumbler lock.

“Moriarty would need supplies,” Reynard mused, his gaze returning to the vast ocean outside the viewport. “Even a secret city inside a volcano cannot be entirely self-sufficient. They would require materials, certain foods, perhaps even new recruits. There must be traffic.”

Frank returned to the control cabin with a new sense of urgency. The mystery was deepening, and the danger felt more palpable with every knot they traveled.

“Masther Frank!” he yelled, his voice sharp with excitement. “A ship! Dead ahead, maybe ten miles off, and she’s makin’ smoke like a factory!”

Frank and Reynard rushed to the forward rail. The young inventor raised his own powerful spyglass to his eye. He saw it at once. It was a long, narrow steamer, painted a dull, non-reflective black from stem to stern. It flew no flag. It cut through the water at a tremendous speed, far faster than any ordinary merchantman.

“That’s no trading vessel,” Frank muttered, adjusting the focus. The decks were clear of the usual clutter of a cargo ship. Instead, he could make out figures moving with military precision, and the glint of the sun on what looked like a strange piece of ordnance mounted on the foredeck. “She matches the description, Reynard. Fast, unmarked, and out of the shipping lanes.”

The projectile screamed past the Pegasus, missing them by less than a hundred feet. It struck the water with a colossal hiss, and a huge plume of steam erupted, as if a meteor had fallen into the sea.

“An electrical bolt of some kind!” Frank gasped, his scientific mind reeling at the sight. “They have harnessed directed energy as a weapon! Moriarty’s genius is even greater than I feared.”

“We cannot let them use that again!” shouted Reynard. “They could cripple us with one hit!”

“They won’t get the chance!” Frank replied, his jaw set. “Barney, target their rudder and propeller! Don’t sink her! I want to take her crew prisoner. They may have the answers we need.”

“As ye say, Masther Frank!”

The Pegasus swooped down like a hawk upon its prey. Barney sighted the dynamite gun, a weapon of Frank’s own design that could fire a small, powerful charge with pinpoint accuracy. The gun boomed, and a shell arced through the air. It exploded just aft of the steamer, sending up a mountain of white water. The vessel shuddered violently from the concussion.

The men on the black ship were not idle. They opened fire with rifles that spat bullets at a phenomenal rate, far faster than any known weapon. The lead pellets pattered against the hardened aluminum hull of the Pegasus like hailstones, making a dreadful racket but doing no serious harm.

Again, the electric cannon charged, a green aura growing around its muzzle.

“Fire again, Barney! Quick!” Frank commanded.

This time, the Irishman’s aim was true. The dynamite shell struck the water directly beneath the steamer’s stern. There was a tremendous bang, and the ship’s fantail was lifted clean out of the water. A great cheer went up from Barney and Pomp as they saw the vessel’s propeller, now mangled and twisted, spinning uselessly in the air. The black ship lost all headway and began to drift helplessly in the waves.

“She’s crippled!” Pomp yelled from the wheelhouse.

“Good work, all!” Frank called out. “Take us down, Pomp. Let’s see what these gentlemen have to say for themselves.”

The Pegasus descended until she hovered a mere fifty feet above the stricken vessel. Frank picked up his speaking trumpet.

“Ahoy, the steamer!” he boomed. “You are disabled and at our mercy! Surrender your vessel and you will be treated as prisoners of war! Resist, and we will sink you!”

“The fanatics!” Reynard breathed, lowering his rifle. “To destroy themselves, their ship, everything, just to protect a secret.”

They had won the battle, but the victory felt hollow. They had learned nothing, save for the terrifying fact that they were facing an enemy whose devotion was as absolute as it was deadly.

“There will be no prisoners to question,” Frank said quietly, his eyes fixed on the spot where the ship had disappeared. “We are on our own. Set course for Hawaii, Pomp. We waste no more time.”

Two days later, the majestic, cloud-wreathed peaks of the Hawaiian Islands rose from the sea. Frank guided the Pegasus to a high altitude, concealing her in a layer of cirrus clouds as they approached the largest island of the chain.

“Mauna Loa and Kilauea,” Frank said, pointing down at the two massive shield volcanoes that dominated the landscape. “The notes mentioned Erebus, the gateway to the underworld in Greek myth, a place of darkness and fire. It has to be one of them.”

For an entire day, they flew careful, systematic patterns over the vast, desolate lava fields. The slopes were a bewildering maze of black rock, ancient flows, and deep fissures. An army could hide here and never be found.

“It’s like lookin’ for a needle in a haystack the size of Ireland,” Barney complained, rubbing his tired eyes.

“We need a better way,” Frank declared. He disappeared into his laboratory and emerged a short while later with a curious device. It consisted of a brass casing with a large, sensitive needle under glass, connected by wires to a long, trailing antenna.

“What’s that contrivance, Masther Frank?” Barney asked.

“I call it a magneto-electric indicator,” the young inventor explained. “A city, even one hidden underground, would require a vast amount of metal. Generators, machinery, structural supports. Such a large mass of iron and steel should create a subtle disturbance in the Earth’s magnetic field. This device is sensitive enough to detect it.”

He switched on the apparatus. For hours, the needle barely quivered. They flew over miles of barren rock, the landscape a uniform, monotonous black. Pomp kept the airship steady, while Barney and Reynard scanned the ground below. Frank’s eyes never left the dial.

They were making a pass over the southeastern flank of Mauna Loa, an area of relatively recent lava flows, when the needle suddenly jumped.

“Look!” Frank cried, his voice electric with excitement. “A deflection! A strong one!”

He directed Pomp to circle the area. The needle grew more and more agitated, finally holding steady, pointing directly down at a wide, flat expanse of pahoehoe lava that looked as solid as the rest of the mountain.

“It’s down there,” Frank said, his voice a whisper of awe. “Directly beneath us.”

There was no sign of an entrance. No cave, no door, not even a crack. It was a seamless wall of volcanic rock.

“We will land in that valley to the west,” Frank commanded, pointing to a small, green cleft in the mountainside a few miles away. “We will camouflage the Pegasus and proceed on foot. We go in tonight, under the cover of darkness.”

The hours that followed were filled with tense preparation. They landed the great airship as gently as a feather in the secluded valley. They covered her with camouflage netting interwoven with branches and large ferns until she blended perfectly with the surrounding jungle. Each man checked his weapons: rifles for Barney, Pomp, and Reynard, and for Frank, his favorite multi-shot electric pistol, another of his own inventions.

As dusk settled, casting long, purple shadows across the mountain, the four adventurers set out. The hike was arduous, over sharp, treacherous a’a lava and slippery, rock-strewn slopes. Finally, they reached the spot their detector had indicated. It was just as it had appeared from the air: a flat, forbidding plain of black rock, gleaming dully in the moonlight.

“Begorra, are ye positive, Masther Frank?” Barney whispered, looking around at the utter desolation. “There’s nothin’ here but rocks and more rocks.”

“The instrument was positive,” Frank insisted. He began to search the ground, running his hands over the smooth, undulating surface. Reynard and Pomp fanned out, their eyes scanning for any anomaly.

For nearly an hour they searched. Their hope was beginning to wane when Frank let out a sharp cry. “Here! I’ve found it!”

The others rushed to his side. He was pointing at the rock face of a low cliff that bordered the lava field. To the naked eye, there was nothing. But when Frank ran his fingers along it, they could see a hairline crack, finer than a spider’s thread, describing the outline of a massive rectangle. It was a work of masonry so perfect it was nearly invisible.

“Incredible,” Reynard breathed. “The skill is beyond belief.”

Frank followed the crack with his fingers until he found a small, almost imperceptible depression near the base. It was no bigger than a silver dollar.

“This must be it,” he said, his heart hammering against his ribs. He pulled the strange, cog-toothed key from his pocket. He fit the key into the depression. It slid in with a soft, satisfying click.

Taking a deep breath, he gripped the key and turned it.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then, a low grinding sound came from deep within the rock, the sound of immense gears turning. The hairline crack widened. Slowly, majestically, a ten ton slab of solid rock began to slide inward, revealing a perfectly square tunnel beyond.

The tunnel was not a rough-hewn cave. It was lined with sheets of polished steel and illuminated by a series of glowing electric lamps set flush into the ceiling, casting a steady, shadowless light. It stretched away into the darkness of the mountain.

The four friends stared in stunned silence. Before them lay the impossible, the stuff of myth and legend.

“This is it,” Frank said, his voice hushed with a mixture of dread and exhilaration. “The gateway to Erebus.”

Rifle at the ready, he took the first step across the threshold. Barney, Pomp, and Reynard followed close behind, their faces grim and determined. They had taken no more than a dozen steps into the metallic corridor when, with a deep thud, the great stone door began to slide shut behind them.

“Look out!” Pomp shouted.

They spun around, but it was too late. The massive slab sealed the entrance with a sound of finality, plunging the world outside into darkness and trapping them within the mountain. A faint click echoed down the corridor as some unseen lock engaged.

“We’re trapped!” Barney exclaimed, rattling the seamless stone door. “It won’t budge!”

“Save your strength,” Reynard advised, his calm demeanor a stark contrast to the Irishman’s agitation. “That door will not be opened from this side.”

From the far end of the long, brightly lit corridor, a new sound arose. It was not the sound of footsteps, but a rhythmic, metallic clanking, heavy and deliberate. Clank. Clank. Clank.

A figure emerged from the distant shadows. It was the shape of a man, but it moved with an unnatural, gliding precision. As it drew closer, the electric light glinted off a body made not of flesh, but of burnished brass and gleaming steel. It was an automaton, a mechanical man seven feet tall. Its head was a smooth metal dome, and where its eyes should have been, two crimson lenses glowed with a malevolent, internal fire.

The automaton stopped a hundred feet away, its head swiveling to fix them with its glowing gaze.

“Be ther powers,” Barney whispered, his face pale. “What divil’s work is this?”

The metal man raised its right arm. With a series of sharp clicks, the hand retracted into the forearm, and a long, wicked-looking barrel extended in its place. The red eyes seemed to brighten as it took aim.

“Down!” Frank yelled, shoving his companions toward the side of the corridor as the automaton’s weapon began to hum with a deadly, rising whine.

“Good work, all!” Frank called out. “Take us down, Pomp. Let’s see what these gentlemen have to say for themselves.”

“I call it a magneto-electric indicator,” the young inventor explained. “A city, even one hidden underground, would require a vast amount of metal. Generators, machinery, structural supports. Such a large mass of iron and steel should create a subtle disturbance in the Earth’s magnetic field. This device is sensitive enough to detect it.”

He switched on the apparatus. For hours, the needle barely quivered. They flew over miles of barren rock, the landscape a uniform, monotonous black. Pomp kept the airship steady, while Barney and Reynard scanned the ground below. Frank’s eyes never left the dial.

They were making a pass over the southeastern flank of Mauna Loa, an area of relatively recent lava flows, when the needle suddenly jumped.

“Look!” Frank cried, his voice electric with excitement. “A deflection! A strong one!”

He directed Pomp to circle the area. The needle grew more and more agitated, finally holding steady, pointing directly down at a wide, flat expanse of pahoehoe lava that looked as solid as the rest of the mountain.

“It’s down there,” Frank said, his voice a whisper of awe. “Directly beneath us.”

There was no sign of an entrance. No cave, no door, not even a crack. It was a seamless wall of volcanic rock.

“We will land in that valley to the west,” Frank commanded, pointing to a small, green cleft in the mountainside a few miles away. “We will camouflage the Pegasus and proceed on foot. We go in tonight, under the cover of darkness.”

They covered her with camouflage netting interwoven with branches and large ferns until she blended perfectly with the surrounding jungle. Each man checked his weapons: rifles for Barney, Pomp, and Reynard, and for Frank, his favorite multi-shot electric pistol, another of his own inventions.

As dusk settled, casting long, purple shadows across the mountain, the four adventurers set out. The hike was arduous, over sharp, treacherous a’a lava and slippery, rock-strewn slopes. Finally, they reached the spot their detector had indicated. It was just as it had appeared from the air: a flat, forbidding plain of black rock, gleaming dully in the moonlight.

“Begorra, are ye positive, Masther Frank?” Barney whispered, looking around at the utter desolation. “There’s nothin’ here but rocks and more rocks.”

“The instrument was positive,” Frank insisted. He began to search the ground, running his hands over the smooth, undulating surface. Reynard and Pomp fanned out, their eyes scanning for any anomaly.

For nearly an hour they searched. Their hope was beginning to wane when Frank let out a sharp cry. “Here! I’ve found it!”

The others rushed to his side. He was pointing at the rock face of a low cliff that bordered the lava field. To the naked eye, there was nothing. But when Frank ran his fingers along it, they could see a hairline crack, finer than a spider’s thread, describing the outline of a massive rectangle. It was a work of masonry so perfect it was nearly invisible.

“Incredible,” Reynard breathed. “The skill is beyond belief.”

Frank followed the crack with his fingers until he found a small, almost imperceptible depression near the base. It was no bigger than a silver dollar.

“This must be it,” he said, his heart hammering against his ribs. He pulled the strange, cog-toothed key from his pocket. He fit the key into the depression. It slid in with a soft, satisfying click.

Taking a deep breath, he gripped the key and turned it.

For a moment, nothing happened. Then, a low grinding sound came from deep within the rock, the sound of immense gears turning. The hairline crack widened. Slowly, majestically, a ten ton slab of solid rock began to slide inward, revealing a perfectly square tunnel beyond.

The tunnel was not a rough-hewn cave. It was lined with sheets of polished steel and illuminated by a series of glowing electric lamps set flush into the ceiling, casting a steady, shadowless light. It stretched away into the darkness of the mountain.

The four friends stared in stunned silence. Before them lay the impossible, the stuff of myth and legend.

“This is it,” Frank said, his voice hushed with a mixture of dread and exhilaration. “The gateway to Erebus.”

Rifle at the ready, he took the first step across the threshold. Barney, Pomp, and Reynard followed close behind, their faces grim and determined. They had taken no more than a dozen steps into the metallic corridor when, with a deep thud, the great stone door began to slide shut behind them.

“Look out!” Pomp shouted.

They spun around, but it was too late. The massive slab sealed the entrance with a sound of finality, plunging the world outside into darkness and trapping them within the mountain. A faint click echoed down the corridor as some unseen lock engaged.

“We’re trapped!” Barney exclaimed, rattling the seamless stone door. “It won’t budge!”

“Save your strength,” Reynard advised, his calm demeanor a stark contrast to the Irishman’s agitation. “That door will not be opened from this side.”

From the far end of the long, brightly lit corridor, a new sound arose. It was not the sound of footsteps, but a rhythmic, metallic clanking, heavy and deliberate. Clank. Clank. Clank.

A figure emerged from the distant shadows. It was the shape of a man, but it moved with an unnatural, gliding precision. As it drew closer, the electric light glinted off a body made not of flesh, but of burnished brass and gleaming steel. It was an automaton, a mechanical man seven feet tall. Its head was a smooth metal dome, and where its eyes should have been, two crimson lenses glowed with a malevolent, internal fire.

The automaton stopped a hundred feet away, its head swiveling to fix them with its glowing gaze.

“Be ther powers,” Barney whispered, his face pale. “What divil’s work is this?”

The metal man raised its right arm. With a series of sharp clicks, the hand retracted into the forearm, and a long, wicked-looking barrel extended in its place. The red eyes seemed to brighten as it took aim.

“Down!” Frank yelled, shoving his companions toward the side of the corridor as the automaton’s weapon began to hum with a deadly, rising whine.

His gaze fell upon a single, large lever, larger than all the others, set apart and painted a stark, warning red. Beside it, etched into the brass plate, was a symbol he recognized instantly: a jagged lightning bolt. “Reynard, Pomp, get up on that console!” he ordered, pointing to the wide shelf below the dials. “Barney, climb on top of that cabinet! Off the floor, all of you! Now!” His friends, seeing the desperate urgency in his eyes, did not question him. They scrambled onto the designated surfaces, their boots leaving the steel floor. “Masther Frank, what are ye about to do?” Barney called down, perched precariously atop a humming metal box. “I am going to give these tin soldiers a shock!” Frank declared, his hand gripping the red lever. The first automaton stepped into the room. Its crimson eye fixed on Frank. Its weapon began to whine. With a mighty heave, Frank threw the lever down. There was a tremendous crackle, and a deep, resonant hum filled the entire mountain. The steel plates of the floor glowed with a sudden, blue-white light. The automaton that had stepped into the room froze instantly. A shower of brilliant blue sparks erupted from its joints. It shuddered violently for a moment, then its single eye went dark, and it crashed to the floor with a deafening clang. Out in the corridor, the same fate befell its brethren. One by one they spasmed, sparked, and then toppled over like so many tin toys, their internal mechanisms fused and destroyed by the massive surge of electrical power Frank had unleashed. The blue glow on the floor faded. The deep hum subsided. Silence returned, broken only by the soft ticking of the dials on the wall. Frank pulled the lever back to its original position. “It is safe to come down now,” he said, wiping a bead of sweat from his brow. His friends cautiously climbed down, staring in awe at the felled giants. “Begorra, Frank, me boy, ye’ve done it again!” Barney cheered, slapping the young inventor on the back so hard he nearly knocked him over. “Ye fried them to a fare-thee-well!” “That was a stroke of genius, Frank,” Reynard said, his usual composure tinged with admiration. “You used their own power source against them.” “It was a gamble,” Frank admitted. “But it was the only chance we had. This entire complex must be the work of the man Murdock serves. The one they call Erebus.” “A man who can build an army of mechanical men is a foe more dangerous than any we have ever faced,” Reyyad mused, nudging a fallen automaton with his boot. “We must be deep inside his main fortress.” “And there’s no goin’ back,” Pomp added, gesturing to the corridor, now blocked with the wreckage of a dozen seven foot automatons, not to mention the sealed stone door far beyond. “The only way is forward.” Frank nodded grimly. “Let’s see what other deviltry lies in wait for us in this mountain.” They proceeded with caution, stepping over the inert bodies of their fallen foes. The corridor continued for another hundred yards before opening out into a space of breathtaking size. They found themselves standing on a high metal catwalk, looking down into a cavern so vast it could have contained a small city. The ceiling was lost in darkness far above, but the cavern floor was brightly lit by hundreds of powerful electric lamps. And what it illuminated made them all gasp. Below them was a factory. Not a factory for cloth or steel, but a factory for producing the very automata they had just fought. Immense assembly lines snaked across the cavern floor. Great cranes and mechanical arms moved with silent precision, lifting brass torsos and attaching steel limbs. Hundreds upon hundreds of automata, in various stages of completion, stood in silent ranks or hung from moving chains. Some were mere skeletons of metal, while others were nearly complete, lacking only their head-domes or crimson eyes. “Saints preserve us,” Barney whispered. “He’s building an army.” “An army that could conquer the world,” Reynard added, his face a grim mask. “Now we know the true nature of Erebus’s plan.” As they watched, transfixed by the horrifying spectacle, Frank’s sharp eyes caught a flicker of movement on a raised platform across the cavern. He pointed. “Look! Over there!” On the platform, which served as the central command post for the entire factory, stood a familiar figure. He was dressed in a fine suit, and he gestured with authority to the silent, working machines below him. “Martin Murdock!” Frank hissed, his hands balling into fists. “So this is where the rascal has been hiding!” Murdock was not alone. He was speaking to a figure on a large viewing screen, a screen so large it dominated the command platform. The figure on the screen was wreathed in shadow, a mere silhouette with two points of cold, piercing light for eyes. The voice that emanated from the screen was deep, resonant, and cold as the grave. “The intruders have breached the outer corridor, Murdock,” the voice of Erebus boomed, echoing slightly in the vast space. “My sentinels have been destroyed.” “A temporary setback, my lord,” Murdock replied, his tone obsequious. “They are trapped within the mountain. The inner patrols will find them. They cannot escape.” “They must not reach the Pegasus,” Erebus commanded. “I have not yet finished my analysis of the young inventor’s remarkable engine. It is a work of genius. I must have its secrets.” “Do not worry, my lord. The airship is secure in the primary hangar bay. They will never get near it.” At the mention of the Pegasus, Frank’s heart gave a leap. His beloved airship was here! It was not destroyed, but captured. A desperate plan began to form in his mind. But as he leaned forward to get a better view, his foot nudged a loose metal bolt lying on the catwalk. The bolt teetered for a moment on the edge, then fell. It clattered down, striking a metal beam below with a loud PING that seemed to echo through the entire cavern. Instantly, all activity on the factory floor below ceased. Every moving crane, every robotic arm, froze in place. Murdock spun around, his eyes scanning the catwalks above. His gaze locked onto the four figures silhouetted against the light. “There!” he shrieked, pointing directly at them. “Intruders! On catwalk seven! Seize them!” The shadowy figure of Erebus on the viewscreen simply said, “Activate the enforcers.” Immediately, a deafening klaxon began to blare. Red lights flashed across the cavern. From alcoves set into the cavern walls, new figures emerged. These were not the standard automata. They were larger, broader, and plated in black, hardened steel. In place of one hand they had a multi-barreled rotary gun, and in place of the other, a vicious-looking pincer claw. “Enforcers!” Murdock cackled from his platform. “Tear them apart!” The enforcers began to ascend the support pillars of the catwalks, their metal claws finding purchase on the beams, climbing with the speed and agility of monstrous insects. “Run!” Frank yelled. They turned and fled back the way they came, but their path was blocked. A half dozen of the black enforcers were dropping down from the ceiling, landing on the catwalk ahead of them. They were trapped. “Down this way!” Reynard shouted, spotting a service ladder leading to a lower level of catwalks. They scrambled down the ladder just as the first enforcer opened fire. A hail of heavy caliber slugs ripped through the spot where they had been standing, shredding the metal grating. They raced along the lower catwalk, the heavy tread of the enforcers echoing all around them. The factory was a maze of gantries and conveyor belts. “Which way, Masther Frank?” Pomp yelled over the din. “The hangar bay!” Frank shouted back. “Murdock said the Pegasus is in the hangar bay! It’s our only way out!” He spotted a large sign with an arrow pointing toward a massive set of blast doors at the far end of the cavern. The sign read: PRIMARY HANGAR. “That way!” They dodged under a moving conveyor belt carrying automaton heads and leaped over another carrying disembodied legs. An enforcer appeared before them, raising its rotary gun. Barney, with a mighty yell, grabbed a long steel pry-bar from a toolbox and hurled it like a spear. The bar flew true, lodging itself in the rotating barrels of the enforcer’s gun. The weapon jammed with a horrible grinding sound and then exploded, sending the enforcer tumbling off the catwalk into the machinery below. They did not stop to celebrate. They ran on, the blast doors of the hangar growing ever closer. Two more enforcers blocked their path, their claws snapping. Frank saw a large control panel for a magnetic crane nearby. While Reynard and Pomp provided covering fire, he sprinted to the panel and slammed his hand down on a large red button. A gigantic electromagnet, hanging from a crane directly above the enforcers, hummed to life. The two black-plated automatons were instantly snatched off their feet and pulled into the air, where they stuck fast to the powerful magnet, flailing helplessly. The path was clear! They sprinted the last fifty yards and threw themselves through the doorway into the hangar bay just as the blast doors began to slide shut behind them. And there she was. Floating gracefully in the center of the immense hangar, held in place by massive docking clamps, was the Pegasus. She was unharmed, gleaming under the bright hangar lights. But she was not unguarded. Standing directly in front of the boarding ramp was the largest automaton they had yet seen. It stood a full twelve feet tall, a veritable colossus of black steel, and in each of its massive hands it held not a gun, but a crackling whip of pure electrical energy. Murdock appeared on an observation balcony high above, a triumphant sneer on his face. “You have been very clever, Mr. Reade,” he called down. “But your journey ends here. Allow me to introduce you to my master’s personal bodyguard. He is quite effective.” The giant automaton took a step forward, swinging its energy whips, which hissed and popped in the air. “Pomp, the emergency tool chest is just inside the main hatch!” Frank yelled. “There’s a woodsman’s axe in there! Get it!” “We can’t get past that thing!” Reynard stated, his rifle looking like a peashooter against such a foe. “We must! Barney, Reynard, keep it distracted! Aim for its joints!” The detective and the Irishman opened fire, their bullets sparking harmlessly against the giant’s armored legs. But it was enough to draw its attention. While the colossus focused on them, Pomp made a desperate dash for the ramp. He dodged a swing from one of the energy whips that cracked against the floor, leaving a blackened, smoking furrow. He leaped up the ramp and vanished into the Pegasus. The automaton turned its attention back to Frank, its optical sensors glowing a menacing purple. It raised both whips to strike. “Pomp, now!” Frank screamed. Pomp reappeared at the hatch, a heavy, double-bitted axe in his hands. He did not hesitate. With a powerful roar, he leaped from the ramp, not at the automaton itself, but at a thick, heavily insulated power cable that snaked across the floor from the wall to the automaton’s leg. With all his strength, he brought the axe down. The blade bit deep into the cable’s insulation. There was a colossal flash of light and a sound like a thunderclap. Every light in the hangar flickered and died for a second, plunging them into momentary darkness. When the lights came back on, the giant automaton was frozen in place. Smoke poured from its joints. Its purple eyes were dark. Then, with a groan of tortured metal, it toppled forward, crashing to the floor with a ground-shaking impact that cracked the concrete. “To the bridge!” Frank yelled, vaulting over the fallen giant’s leg. They scrambled aboard the Pegasus, their hearts hammering in their chests. Frank did not waste a second, sprinting for the engine room. Barney and Reynard ran for the pilot-house. “The clamps, Frank!” Barney shouted. “We’re still locked in!” “I am on it!” Frank yelled back from below. He threw a series of switches on the auxiliary power board. With a series of loud bangs, the massive docking clamps holding the Pegasus retracted. A moment later, the familiar, powerful hum of the dynamo filled the airship, and the great helices above began to spin, slowly at first, then with increasing speed. The Pegasus lifted gracefully from her cradle. Murdock watched from the balcony, his face a mask of fury. He ran to a control panel and slammed his fist on a large red button. A new, earsplitting alarm began to sound. The massive blast doors that led to the outside world began to slide shut. “He is trapping us in!” Reynard shouted from the pilot-house. “We will never break through those doors!” “We will not have to!” Frank yelled, climbing the ladder to the pilot-house. He took the controls from Barney. “The roof! There must be launch doors in the roof!” He sent the Pegasus soaring upward. High above, a section of the cavern roof, marked with yellow and black stripes, began to part. A circle of blue sky appeared. “He’s opening it!” Barney cried. “He means to let us out!” “It is a trap!” Frank countered, his eyes narrowed. He pointed to the side of the hangar, where a series of strange-looking projectors were rising from the floor and aiming at the opening. “Those are magnetic harpoons! He means to let us get halfway out and then snag us!” The opening was now fully dilated. Freedom was just a few hundred feet above them. Murdock stood on his balcony, a cruel smile on his face, his hand hovering over another button. “Barney, the forward gun!” Frank commanded. “Load it with a shell! Pomp, help him!” The two men scrambled for the deck-house where the rapid-fire signal gun was mounted. “Aim for Murdock’s control panel!” Frank shouted, keeping the Pegasus hovering just below the deadly range of the harpoon launchers. “If you destroy it, he cannot fire them!” Barney swiveled the small cannon around, peering through the sights. Murdock and his control panel were a small target, a hundred yards away. “Faith, an’ it’s a divil of a shot, Masther Frank!” Barney yelled back, his hands flying as he and Pomp loaded a small, explosive shell. “Can ye do it?” “I can try!” Murdock saw what they were doing. His smile vanished. He lunged for the firing button. “Fire, Barney!” Frank roared, pushing the engines to their limit and sending the Pegasus hurtling toward the opening in the roof. “Fire now!”
